headline: US tariff reset after Supreme Court ruling leaves Malaysia worse off
context: The US Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs on 20 February 2026. A 10% surcharge followed, and in March USTR named Malaysia among 16 economies in a Section 301 excess-capacity probe. Malaysia's trade minister called the ART deal void.

changes.summary: Correction: Earlier editions said the US Supreme Court voided the US-Malaysia trade deal, that Section 301 probes do not target chips and that US firms make 68% of Malaysia's chip exports; the Court held that IEEPA does not authorise tariffs and Malaysia's trade minister then called the deal void, the US probe that names Malaysia lists semiconductors, and 65% of chips exported to the US come from American firms.

Correction: we removed four statements we could not confirm against a source, on patronage, tariff dodging, local supplier numbers and Sabah and Sarawak's exposure, and a claim about past governments' trade choices. The forced-labour card now notes that Malaysia is among the 60 economies investigated.

cards.big: The US Supreme Court struck down Trump's IEEPA tariffs on 20 February. Within a month, Malaysia faced a new surcharge and a Section 301 probe.
cards.sub: The 10% surcharge runs for 150 days. Section 301 duties have no fixed time limit or rate cap. Malaysia's trade minister then called the ART 'null and void'.

cards.big: The Court ruled IEEPA does not authorise tariffs. Section 301 does: USTR may impose duties 'for such time as' it deems appropriate, with no maximum rate.
cards.sub: USTR's excess-capacity probe covers 16 economies, Malaysia included. Example sectors include semiconductors, solar modules, steel and aluminium.

cards.big: Chips make up 68% of Malaysia's E&E exports to the US, and American firms operating here ship 65% of those chips, then-trade minister Tengku Zafrul said in August 2025.
cards.sub: So most of the chips a US semiconductor tariff would hit are shipped by American companies operating in Malaysia.

cards.big: A forced-labour probe across 60 economies, Malaysia among them, hands the US a second front.
The court victory was a trap. IEEPA tariffs fell, and Section 301 duties, if imposed, carry no fixed time limit or rate cap.
The vulnerability is real but leverage is underestimated. Malaysia lacks not options but political will to convert CPTPP, RCEP, and the NSSP into actual strategy.
